title: How fast can a driven Markov network oscillate? A four-state counterexample to the affine Karpelevich conjecture, and the exact dimension at which it fails
shortTitle: A four-state network breaks the affine Karpelevich conjecture
oneLine: The rescaled eigenvalues of Markov rate matrices do not always fill the affinity-squashed Karpelevich region conjectured by Xu, Kolchinsky, Delvenne and Ito (2025): an integer four-state network escapes it, three states cannot, and on fully connected networks every size from four up fails; the single-cycle case remains open.
abstract: The eigenvalues of a continuous-time Markov rate matrix decide how fast its probability distribution relaxes and how strongly it can oscillate. For discrete-time transition matrices the exact set of possible eigenvalues is a classical object, the Karpelevich region Ω_n. Xu, Kolchinsky, Delvenne and Ito (Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 257102, 2025; Supplement Eq. (S3)) conjectured that the eigenvalues of rate matrices fill a squashed copy of this region: stretched by the fastest escape rate α and flattened vertically by β′ = tanh(max_c F_c/(2n_c)), set by the largest cycle affinity per step. This candidate shows the conjecture is false. An explicit four-state network with integer rates and about 8.4 k_BT of driving around its strongest cycle has the eigenvalue −4745 + 450√3 i, whose rescaled image ζ ≈ −0.7062 + 0.3161 i lies 0.0087 above the left boundary arc of Ω₄; one integer inequality proves it. For at most three states the containment holds, so four is the smallest failing size. The mechanism is weak resetting: it moves eigenvalues by O(ε) but relaxes the affinity factor by order ε^{2/3}. This gives counterexamples near a whole boundary arc in four states, an explicit interval 0 < ε ≤ 1/100, exactly certified five- and six-state instances whose data are printed in an appendix and re-checked by a stand-alone checker, and an asymptotic construction in every dimension n ≥ 4. All counterexamples use networks in which every pair of states is connected; whether the conjecture holds for single-cycle networks, the setting in which it was tested, remains open. The violations are thin, and the proved affinity ellipse and Farey-polygon bounds are unaffected. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Four-state counterexample: the integer rate matrix Q_w has eigenvalue −4745 + 450√3 i with α = 2781 and dominant triangle ratio 177853829/38529; its rescaled image ζ ≈ −0.7062 + 0.3161 i lies 0.0087 above the left boundary arc of Ω₄, so Supplement Eq. (S3) of Xu et al. (2025) fails (Proposition 2.1, Theorem 3.1, proof with an exact integer certificate).
Smallest size: for at most three states the rescaled spectrum lies in Ω_n, so four is the smallest failing dimension (Theorem 4.1, proof, using the sector bound of Ohga, Ito and Kolchinsky).

Mechanism: weak resetting moves eigenvalues by O(ε) but relaxes the affinity factor by order ε^{2/3}, giving counterexamples near every point of the open left arc of Ω₄, an explicit interval 0 < ε ≤ 1/100, and an open set of positive-rate counterexamples (Theorems 5.1, 6.1, Corollary 6.2, proof).
Every dimension n ≥ 4 fails on fully connected networks: fix n, then a small t, then let ε → 0; the thresholds are not explicit (Theorem 7.4, proof).
Explicit five- and six-state instances are certified exactly, with the certificate data printed in Appendix A and re-checked by a separate checker (Theorem 7.6, computer-assisted exact certificate).
Open: whether the conjecture holds for single-cycle networks (Open problem 8.1); a small numerical ring search found no violation, which is evidence, not proof.

narration: A four-state network breaks a conjecture about Markov spectra. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the background. Many systems in physics and biology hop at random between a few states, like a molecular motor or a chemical clock. The eigenvalues of the matrix of hopping rates say how fast such a system settles down and how strongly it can oscillate on the way. Oscillation needs a thermodynamic push around a cycle of states. Next, the conjecture. In 2025, Xu, Kolchinsky, Delvenne and Ito proposed an exact map of where these eigenvalues can lie: a classical shape called the Karpelevich region, stretched by the fastest escape rate and squashed vertically by the strongest push per step around any cycle. Now, the main finding. The conjecture is false. An explicit four-state network with whole-number rates has an eigenvalue that, after this rescaling, lands just outside the region, by about nine thousandths. One integer inequality proves it. For three or fewer states the conjecture holds, so four is the smallest failing size. The mechanism is simple. Adding weak resetting moves the eigenvalues only a little, but relaxes the squashing factor much more. The paper uses this to build counterexamples in every size from four upwards, and certifies five- and six-state examples in exact arithmetic, with the data printed so that readers can check it. Finally, the limits. Every counterexample links every pair of states. Whether the conjecture holds for a single ring of states, where it was tested, is still open. The violations are small, and the proved ellipse and polygon bounds are unaffected. This is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, checked by AI-assisted review only, not peer review. Published on 27 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: An integer four-state rate matrix whose rescaled eigenvalue lies outside the Karpelevich region Ω₄ refutes Supplement Eq. (S3) of Xu, Kolchinsky, Delvenne and Ito (2025); containment is proved for n ≤ 3 and fails for every n ≥ 4 on complete graphs, with certified n = 5, 6 instances.
decisionObject.scope: Irreducible continuous-time Markov rate matrices with bidirectional edges; all counterexamples use the complete graph; the single-cycle case is open; thresholds for n ≥ 7 are not explicit.
